Martyrs, Morale, and Militarism: The Political Impact of Devastation and Slaughter Shizuka Inoue, David E. Weinstein, and Atsushi Yamagishi NBER Working Paper No. 33842 May 2025, Revised October 2026 JEL No. D7, H56, N45

## ABSTRACT

Do wars push the communities that suffer them left or right? We argue that the answer depends on the nature of the loss: communities respond differently to losing people and losing places. We show this using data from Japan’s WWII experience, where military deaths, civilian bombing deaths, and urban destruction varied across cities for reasons plausibly unrelated to their politics. Across sixtythree years of elections, cities that lost more soldiers voted disproportionately for Japan’s rightwing, pro-rearmament Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), while cities that suffered more physical destruction voted for left-wing, pacifist parties. Civilian bombing deaths move the vote in the same direction as military deaths. This pattern reconciles why WWI battle deaths pushed interwar Italian and German communities toward the right while building destruction in the Blitz pushed British cities toward the left. Survey, testimony, and organizational data indicate that deaths created “martyrs” whose commemoration benefited the right, whereas devastation durably lowered prowar “morale”. Our estimates imply that absent U.S. area bombing, the LDP would have won the two-thirds majority of Japan’s House of Representatives that is a necessary first step toward revising Japan’s pacifist constitution and rearming.

## 1 Introduction

Do wars push the communities that suﬀer them to the political left or to the right? The answer

matters beyond political history: strategies like “morale bombing” were premised on assumptions

about how devastation reshapes an enemy’s politics, and whether it stabilizes the postwar order by

pacifying the enemy or sows the seeds of future conﬂict. A century of evidence suggests that the

answer can go either way, and the literature has not resolved why. In Italy, Acemoglu et al. (2022)

show that municipalities with high World War I infantry casualty rates swung ﬁrst to the antiwar

Socialists in 1919 and then, within ﬁve years, delivered disproportionate support for Mussolini’s

Fascists. In Germany, De Juan et al. (2024) ﬁnd that counties that lost more of their soldiers voted

persistently for right-wing nationalist parties, including the Nazis, throughout the interwar period,

and Koenig (2023) shows that returning veterans shifted Weimar electorates durably from left to

right. Yet wartime suﬀering does not always feed the right. British cities that endured heavier

German bombing shifted toward Labour (Heldring et al., 2022), civilians on the front lines of

Colombia’s civil war were more willing than their countrymen to support peace and concessions

(Tellez, 2019), and a large literature ﬁnds that civilian victims of wartime violence become more

cooperative and altruistic, not more belligerent (Bauer et al., 2016; Blattman, 2009).

This paper argues that these seemingly contradictory ﬁndings are two sides of the same phe-

nomenon: communities respond in opposite ways to the loss of people and the loss of places.

We make use of novel Japanese WWII data covering nearly a century of elections to show that

deaths—whether of soldiers on distant battleﬁelds or of civilians in bombed cities—durably shifted

electoral constituencies toward Japan’s dominant right-wing party, the Liberal Democratic Party

(LDP), while the physical devastation of the urban landscape durably shifted constituencies toward

the parties of the left. We call the ﬁrst force the “martyr eﬀect”: the dead become sacred, and the

politics of honoring them belongs to the right. We call the second the “morale eﬀect,” after the

“morale bombing” that produced it: living amid ruins durably lowered communities’ identiﬁcation

with the political camp that had led the nation to war. We do not impose these labels on the data: in

over 1,500 wartime testimonies, accounts anchored in a soldier’s death disproportionately frame the

loss through sacriﬁce and honor, while accounts anchored in bombing disproportionately describe

the war as hopeless and futile. Because both forces operated simultaneously, within a single country,

a single conﬂict, and a single party system, Japan lets us separate them—and lets us test, rather than

assume, which dimension of the left–right divide wartime experience actually moved. The result

is that a war that ended eighty years ago continues to shape Japan’s political geography today—in

opposite directions, depending on what each community lost.

Our point of departure from this literature is to unbundle the eﬀects of wartime loss. Each of the

studies above uses variation arising from a single dimension of wartime experience, because each

setting supplied essentially only one source of variation: in WWI Italy and Germany, communities

lost their young men by the hundreds of thousands while their home cities stood untouched, and the

survivors ultimately moved right; in WWII Britain, German bombing damaged about two houses in

every seven while killing comparatively few civilians (Titmuss, 1950, Ch. XVI), and the survivors

moved left. Because deaths and devastation rarely vary independently within a single electorate,

existing evidence cannot tell us whether these opposite responses reﬂect diﬀerent treatments or

diﬀerent countries, wars, and party systems.

Japan provides the missing experiment because it suﬀered both forms of loss on an immense

scale: Japan had nearly as many military casualties in WWII as Germany and Italy had in World

War I combined (Hirota, 1992; Acemoglu et al., 2022; De Juan et al., 2024); U.S. air raids over

Japan killed over ﬁve times as many civilians as German air raids over Britain (Nakamura, ed, 1995;

Titmuss, 1950);1 and U.S. area bombing typically destroyed just over half the buildings in targeted

cities (Davis and Weinstein, 2002). Crucially, the two forms of loss struck diﬀerent places. Japan’s

hometown-based regiment system caused the draft cohorts of some cities to be decimated while

leaving others nearly untouched, and the only land battle on Japanese soil was in Okinawa, which is

excluded from our sample. Conditional on being targeted, civilian death rates varied substantially

military or civilian, pushed communities toward the right, while devastation pushed them toward

the left. The civilian-death eﬀect is less robust than the other two, however, because although there

is enormous variation across cities in the death rates for draft-age men, only two cities—Hiroshima

devastation predicts not only less LDP support, but also more support for the Japanese Communist

share of all opposition votes.

Japanese postwar politics also allows us to interpret the left–right divide with unusual clarity.

Japan’s conservative LDP was explicitly formed to rearm Japan and strengthen security ties with the

U.S., and its opposition advocated left-wing, paciﬁst policies, so the country’s dominant political

cleavage mapped directly onto the questions the war had posed (Section 3.2). Moreover, the super-

majority required to revise the U.S.-imposed constitution banning rearmament kept that cleavage

salient for seventy-ﬁve years as right-wing politicians tried to win enough votes for revision. While

prior work (Ogasawara and Komura, 2022; Asai and Kambayashi, 2023) has shown that gender

ratios at the prefecture level reﬂect battle casualties, we improve on these measures by showing

that this variation can be used to construct estimates of casualty rates at the more disaggregated

municipal level. We follow recent work by Kimura (2023) showing that there was substantial

variation across cities within prefectures to build a municipal dataset with approximately 65 times

as many geographical units as earlier work based on Japan’s 47 prefectures, which we aggregate to

the 300 largest cities for our regressions—still leaving more than six times as many units. Indeed,

all of our identiﬁcation uses a full set of prefectural ﬁxed eﬀects, so our identiﬁcation arises from

the cohorts of prime-age conscripts suﬀered high levels of military casualties, and we show that this

ratio is high in prefectures whose regiments were decimated and low in those whose regiments saw

little combat. We also show that the gender ratios of the adjacent, draft-ineligible cohorts cluster

near the natural ratio and do not predict LDP voting, so the draft-cohort ratio is not simply picking

up local diﬀerences in overall gender ratios.

We implement an approach that addresses many potential omitted variable biases. Our baseline

speciﬁcation explains a city’s right-wing vote share in a given postwar year by the war’s deaths

and devastation, conditioning on the same city’s right-wing vote share in 1928. A salient political

issue in that election was whether Japan should expand its navy. By controlling for votes for

the conservative Seiyukai party, a forerunner of the LDP that also supported expanding Japan’s

military, we control for a city’s inherent right-wing voting behavior. We augment this strategy by

also controlling for a variety of other potential confounding variables.

The political legacies of these wartime losses are also strikingly persistent. Consistent with

Voth (2021) and Ochsner and Roesel (2024),2 we ﬁnd that the martyr and morale eﬀects are present

in essentially every postwar election and show no attenuation over the entire 1958–1993 period,

even though most Japanese with direct experience of the war are no longer alive.3 The legacies

even survived the collapse of the postwar political system itself: after 1993, the LDP brieﬂy lost

power, the electoral system was overhauled, and the opposition was remade, yet both eﬀects, though

attenuated, remain clearly detectable in the new system through 2021.

Nor is this persistence a mystery: the martyr eﬀect is transmitted within families and reinforced

through conservative organizations for the war-bereaved, while the morale eﬀect is likely transmitted

through families and acquaintances but is also institutionalized in the peace education of children

born generations after the ﬁghting stopped. We use extensive data on Japanese attitudes and policies

to show the existence of these channels and explain both voting behavior and the persistence of

We also conduct a simple counterfactual exercise to assess the magnitude of our point estimates.

We examine a scenario in which the U.S. decided not to use area bombing to destroy civilian targets

but instead just targeted the Japanese military. This counterfactual strategy would have reduced

the morale eﬀect in Japanese cities by leaving their structures intact and lowered the martyr eﬀect

arising from the killing of civilians. We ﬁnd that the reduced morale eﬀect dominates, and on

net the greater LDP support would have been large enough to enable the LDP to obtain more

than a two-thirds majority in the Diet’s House of Representatives. Since this has been one of the

major hurdles in achieving constitutional revision, our estimates suggest that the morale eﬀect is

suﬃciently large that it could explain why Japan has not revised its constitution to allow a military.

## 2 Related Literature

In addition to the works already cited, our paper relates to several important strands in the literature.

First, our work is also related to work on how military actions aﬀect guerrilla activities. Kocher et

al. (2011) and Dell and Querubin (2018) examine the impact of bombing near civilian populations

and ﬁnd that it increases insurgent recruitment and activity. Lyall (2009) studied counterinsur-

gency operations in Chechnya, concluding that indiscriminate violence increased local support for

insurgents rather than deterring rebellion. Similarly, Jaeger and Paserman (2008) analyze Israeli

military actions and ﬁnd that targeted killings frequently led to retaliatory violence, reinforcing

militant group cohesion and increasing future attacks. Finally, Dell (2015) explores the unintended

consequences of militarized approaches to drug conﬂicts in Mexico, demonstrating that government

crackdowns on traﬃcking networks often lead to increased cartel violence.

Second, historians and political scientists disagree about the impact of military actions on enemy

morale, deﬁned as the willingness to ﬁght. Pollack (2002) provides evidence that overwhelming

military force can lower morale when it leads to the perception of inevitable defeat, as observed

in several Arab military conﬂicts where high casualties and sustained losses weakened combat

eﬀectiveness. Pape (1996) and Dower (1999) argue that bombing had small eﬀects on morale.

However, scholars such as Grayling (2007), Lyall (2009), and Jaeger and Paserman (2008) emphasize

the morale-hardening eﬀects of indiscriminate violence.

Third, a growing body of work on contemporary conﬂict ﬁnds that civilian exposure to lethal

violence pushes electorates rightward, echoing our martyr eﬀect. Studying Israel, Berrebi and

Klor (2008) show that localities suﬀering more terror fatalities shift toward the right-wing bloc,

an eﬀect they attribute to the right’s ownership of security policy, and Gould and Klor (2010)

likewise ﬁnd that local terror deaths raise right-wing vote shares. Getmansky and Zeitzoﬀ(2014)

ﬁnd that Israeli towns brought within rocket range vote two to six points more for the right. This

literature establishes that civilian victimization can move voters to the right, but it does not separate

the political eﬀect of killing people from that of destroying places: the ﬁrst two studies measure

7


<!-- Page 9 -->


only fatalities and contain no destruction channel, while the third bundles death, damage, and fear

into a single exposure indicator and concedes that it “is unable to adjudicate on whether the main

eﬀect of terrorism on political behavior operates through casualty aversion or through living under

threat” (Getmansky and Zeitzoﬀ, 2014). Because our setting varies deaths and physical destruction

separately, we can draw exactly this distinction, and we ﬁnd that the two move voters in opposite

directions. These settings also diﬀer from ours in that the adversary remains a live threat: a

rightward shift after an attack may there reﬂect a demand for future deterrence, whereas the eﬀects

we document persist for three-quarters of a century after the ﬁghting ended and the wartime enemy

became a close ally, so that they cannot be explained by prospective security concerns and instead

isolate the commemorative legacy of past violence.

Finally, our paper relates to work on the persistence and intergenerational transmission of

political attitudes, and in particular on the role of schooling in reproducing them. Voigtländer and

Voth (2015) show that Germans educated under the Nazi regime remained two to three times more

anti-Semitic than adjacent cohorts decades later, demonstrating that state schooling can durably

instill political beliefs. Consistent with this, Cantoni et al. (2017) ﬁnd that a curriculum reform

in China shifted students’ political attitudes, Clots-Figueras and Masella (2013) ﬁnd that bilingual

schooling raised Catalan national identity and support for nationalist parties, and Fouka (2020) shows

that prohibiting German-language instruction in U.S. schools after World War I durably shaped the

ethnic identiﬁcation of aﬀected children; Lott (1999) argues more broadly that governments invest

in public schooling partly to instill loyalty and shape political preferences. Our peace-education

results (Section 6) document the same channel operating in the opposite ideological direction:

schools in more heavily bombed communities transmit an antimilitarist outlook to children born

long after the war, helping explain why the morale eﬀect persists across generations.

## 3 Right-Wing Politics in Japan

In the postwar period, the LDP has been Japan’s right-of-center party, favoring more market-oriented

policies than its historical opponents, the Japan Socialist and Communist Parties, as well as their

8


<!-- Page 10 -->


more recent successors. Less well known outside Japan is that the clearest diﬀerence between the

LDP and its opposition concerns national defense. In this respect, Japan resembles the interwar

settings against which we compare it: in Italy and in Weimar Germany, whatever else divided

the parties, the political right was the pro-military pole. This section documents that Japanese

politics has been organized the same way for a century, with the conservative LDP and its prewar

predecessors on the pro-military side and the opposition on the paciﬁst side, and that voters have

understood it that way. Section 3.1 describes the 1928 baseline our design exploits, and Section 3.2

shows that the postwar LDP was assembled around rearmament and that the constitutional bar to

rearmament kept the issue salient throughout our sample period.

### 3.1 Militarism and Voting Before World War II

The ﬁrst election after the passage of the 1925 Universal Male Suﬀrage Act, which granted the vote

to adult men, centered on national defense issues. Tanaka Giichi, a former army general, became

president of the Rikken Seiyukai or “Friends of the Constitution Party” in 1925 and espoused pro-

military, imperialist attitudes. Tanaka advocated “popularizing national defense” and ﬁnding a way

for Japan to “break free from its insular position, become a continental state, and conﬁdently extend

its national power” (Duus, ed, 1988, pp. 94 and 275). The Seiyukai won the 1928 general election

on a platform of strong opposition to arms control. Because the 1928 contest centered heavily on

whether Japan should pursue military expansion, we use a city’s Seiyukai vote share as a prewar

benchmark for its inherited pro-military leaning and control throughout our analysis, separating

the eﬀect of wartime loss from a community’s inherited politics. We describe the benchmark as

pro-military rather than right-wing because the Seiyukai and LDP were not always conservative,

in the classical sense, on economic policy: both periodically favored expansionary budgets, loose

monetary policy, and rural public works (Metzler, 2006, pp. 67–68, 183).5

### 3.2 Militarism and the Liberal Democratic Party

For our purposes, the postwar LDP’s clearest distinguishing feature was its goals of rearmament

and constitutional revision, while its principal opponents deﬁned themselves by opposition to both.

This subsection documents that alignment and its stability over time, because it enables us to use a

city’s LDP vote share as a measure of its residents’ pro-military sentiment.

The lineage runs directly from the prewar party. After Japan’s defeat, the Seiyukai reorganized

itself into a pro-rearmament Liberal Party under Hatoyama Ichiro. From the ﬁrst general election

after the U.S. occupation ended, in October 1952, rearmament and revision of the U.S.-imposed

constitution banning Japan’s military were conspicuous in every campaign: Hatoyama favored

both, the Socialists opposed both, and Prime Minister Yoshida sought a middle ground of gradual

self-defense capacity without amendment (Ward, 1956, p. 50).6 In 1954, Hatoyama became Prime

Minister and formed the LDP the following year by bringing together Diet members who favored

rearmament. The party’s founding document made its position clear: “the primary focus of the

early occupation policy was on weakening our nation . . . We will establish self-defense forces

commensurate with national strength and circumstances under a collective security system, prepar-

ing for the withdrawal of foreign military forces stationed in Japan” (Liberal Democratic Party,

1955). Six decades later, Japan’s longest-serving Prime Minister, Abe Shinzo, described the party’s

origins the same way: “The Liberals and Democrats who formed the LDP wanted to create our

own constitution, and the merger of the two parties was done to achieve the two-thirds majority in

both houses that was needed for revision. Revising the constitution was the symbol of our regained

independence. It was for this that the Liberal Democratic Party was founded” (Council on Foreign

Relations, n.d.).

The salience of the LDP’s pro-military position probably peaked in 1960, when massive protests

The new treaty enabled the U.S. and Japan to maintain military forces in Japan, which could be used

to attack third countries, and contained an article stating that the U.S. and Japan should “maintain

and develop, subject to their constitutional provisions, their capacities to resist armed attack” (Japan

constitution. In the ensuing protests, hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets, forcing

President Eisenhower to cancel his trip to Japan. Despite the unrest, the LDP scored its biggest

electoral success in the November 1960 general election, winning 296 of the 467 seats in the lower

house—over 60 percent—on 57.6 percent of the popular vote, and ushering in what the Japanese

call the “1955 System”: the one-party dominance of the LDP, which maintained control of the

lower house of the Diet until 1993. However, a constitutional amendment remained out of reach:

it required two-thirds of both the lower and upper houses and approval in a national referendum,

and left-wing parties denied the LDP the supermajority needed even to begin. This situation made

constitutional amendment a salient diﬀerence between the LDP and other parties throughout our

sample period: a fact that enables us to use the LDP vote share as a measure of voters’ pro-military

attitudes.

While constitutional revision is an important diﬀerence between the LDP and its opposition,

many other issues inﬂuence Japanese election outcomes, and voters’ views on revision are not a

litmus test for which party they support. Indeed, the existence of other issues helps to motivate

the error term in our analysis. The surveys we present here establish only that the LDP occupies

the pro-military pole of this cleavage, validating the LDP vote share as our outcome; the separate

question of how wartime loss pushed communities toward one pole or the other is taken up in

Section 6. LDP politicians are surprisingly uniﬁed on the issue of constitutional revision—only 2

percent support leaving the constitution unchanged (Ogi, 2024)—and Figure 1 shows that between

2003 and 2022 they were, on average, far more supportive than other politicians of strengthening

## 4 Data

We bring several novel datasets to bear on how wartime loss reshaped voting. Our analysis rests

on three exposure measures that map onto the paper’s central distinction between losing people and

losing places: military deaths and civilian bombing deaths—the loss of people, which we argue

produced the martyr eﬀect—and the destruction of the built environment—the loss of places, which

produced the morale eﬀect. We relate these to nearly a century of Japanese election results, which

let us measure a city’s voting before and after its soldiers, citizens, or structures were killed or

destroyed. Our death and destruction data are far more disaggregated than any used before, linking

wartime loss to electoral outcomes at the city level.7 Section 4.3 explains how the 1994 electoral

reform changes both the measure of LDP support and the periods over which we report results;

Section 4.4 describes how we construct the military-death measure and Section 4.5 the two air-raid

measures, which, though they arise from the same raids, may push voting in opposite directions.

### 4.3 The 1993–94 Institutional Break

The collapse of the “1955 System” in 1993–94 allows us to test whether the wartime political

legacies persisted after a major institutional change. The LDP had governed continuously since its

formation in 1955, with the Japan Socialist Party (JSP) as its principal opposition. The bursting of

Japan’s stock and land-price bubbles weakened the LDP and allowed a non-LDP coalition to take

oﬃce after the 1993 election, and the new government enacted a major electoral reform in 1994.

The reform changed both electoral competition and how we measure party support. Before 1994,

House of Representatives members were elected from multi-member districts under a single non-

transferable vote, which required candidates from the same party to compete against one another.

15


<!-- Page 17 -->


The reform replaced this system with a combination of single-member constituencies (SMCs) and

proportional representation constituencies (PRCs), so voters now cast one ballot for a constituency

candidate and another for a party. We therefore measure post-reform LDP support using the

proportional-representation vote, which most directly captures support for the party. PRC elections

account for about 38 percent of lower-house Diet members and are the most comparable post-reform

electoral counterpart to the party-level vote totals we construct for the pre-reform period.

The break also transformed party competition. The JSP ceased to be the LDP’s principal

opposition, opposition parties repeatedly reorganized, and the LDP returned to government through

new coalition arrangements: ﬁrst with the JSP and later with the more paciﬁst Clean Government

Party, which moderated the coalition’s constitutional-revision agenda (Samuels, 2004). Together,

these changes let us ask whether the legacies we document survive a wholesale institutional break,

and they are the reason we report results separately for the pre-reform (1958–1993) and post-reform

(1996–2021) periods throughout.

### 4.4 The Causes and Measurement of Military Fatalities

The value of the military-death exposure variable underlying the martyr eﬀect rests on two claims.

First, we argue that military logistics, rather than community characteristics, determined which

cities experienced high rates of military deaths. Second, we argue that city-level soldier death rates

varied suﬃciently to allow reliable imputation from the postwar census.

The Imperial Japanese Army (IJA) formed infantry regiments by recruiting men from the city

or county where they lived.11 Asai and Kambayashi (2023) argue that the allocation of regiments

to battleﬁelds was exogenous, meaning a regiment’s survival probability was unrelated to future

voting in its hometown. Because the IJA often did not know which islands would be attacked,

regiments sent to major battleﬁelds such as Iwo Jima and Okinawa had death rates close to 100

percent, while those stationed in Korea, Taiwan, or the Japanese mainland saw little to no ﬁghting.

The IJA deployed regiments based on training, experience, and battle fatigue, whereas American

<!-- Page 18 -->


battle plans depended on the importance of the islands rather than on where soldiers lived before

enlisting.

A second, and probably more important, source was the U.S. policy of “unrestricted submarine

warfare,” announced on December 7, 1941, and the later “Operation Starvation,” which together

sank 81 percent of Japan’s ship tonnage (Davis and Weinstein, 2008). Rather than dislodging

Japanese troops through battle, these operations severed their food and military supply lines.

Because passengers on torpedoed ships were rarely rescued, entire regiments were often eliminated

in transit.12 Yoshida (2017) ﬁnds that 60 percent of all Japanese military deaths were caused by

starvation and disease. Such rates are hard to reconcile with expectations about postwar voting, so

we treat the variation they generate as exogenous. Which hometowns were aﬀected also depended

on decisions unrelated to the soldiers themselves. The 145th Regiment from Kagoshima was sent

to Iwo Jima, where only 162 of its 2,727 soldiers survived, while the 24th Regiment from Fukuoka

was stationed in Taiwan and, therefore, saw no combat. These cases make it unlikely that any other

variable explaining postwar voting is correlated with which municipalities suﬀered high casualty

rates.

Because soldier death rates were never recorded at the city level, we infer them from census data.

Asai and Kambayashi (2023) use prefectural variation in gender ratios for draft-aged cohorts as a

proxy. However, Kimura (2023, pp. 17–19) shows that Japanese regiments were often organized

by ﬁner geographic units, i.e., the city (“shi”) or the county (“gun”) in which they lived.13 We

therefore construct city-level gender ratios for the draft cohort using the 1950 Population Census.

Japanese men between 17 and 40 could be drafted (Watanabe, 2022), and boys as young as 14 could

“volunteer”; service rates by birth cohort imply a lower bound on military service of roughly 15

years of age in 1945 (see Appendix A.8.3).

The variation in this ratio across places is more important for our purposes, and much of it

We obtained our data on air raid deaths and building destruction from Davis and Weinstein

of buildings destroyed as a result of U.S. “area bombing” of Japanese cities. We deﬁne “Per-Capita

An important issue concerns the measurement and exogeneity of the devastation caused by

bombing. While historical accounts suggest that which regiment was sent to which potential

battleﬁeld was exogenous, U.S. targeting decisions may have relied on variables correlated with

future LDP support. The U.S. initially targeted Tokyo, Yokohama, Kawasaki, Nagoya, Kobe, and

Osaka based on “industrial importance” and radar signal strength (which enabled low-altitude night

raids) (Craven and Cate, 1953, pp. 610 and 624). Thereafter, Japan’s smaller cities were targeted

based on ﬁve criteria: “1) congestion and inﬂammability; 2) incidence of war industry; 3) incidence

of transportation facilities; 4) size and population; and 5) adaptability to radar bombing” (Craven

and Cate, 1953, p. 653). War industry was typically deﬁned as the presence of aircraft, shipbuilding,

and weapons manufacturing plants, as well as the manufacturing plants that provided inputs. The

fact that size and population were important criteria might threaten identiﬁcation because large

cities tend to have more manufacturing ﬁrms and might have diﬀerent support rates for the LDP.

In addition, per-capita building destruction is an imperfect measure of the devastation residents

experienced—the line between a destroyed building and a damaged one, for example, is not always

clear in the underlying counts—and such measurement error attenuates OLS estimates of the morale

eﬀect toward zero.

We therefore also use data on the number of munitions factories and the share of manufacturing

employment in a city as instruments for per-capita building destruction, addressing both concerns

(see Appendix A.1.10 for details). Our identifying assumption is that, conditional on our controls,

the historical placement of munitions factories and urban manufacturing employment shares predict

bombing intensity but do not independently predict postwar politics. This view is supported

by Kotani (2025), which shows that the location of prewar manufacturing plants was heavily

inﬂuenced by water-power sources, a factor unlikely to matter for postwar politics.16 Our estimates

We adopt some semantic conventions to facilitate discussing the issues. First, right-wing Japanese

refer to Japan’s war dead as “martyrs” (e.g., showa junnansha), so we use the term “martyr eﬀect”

These two patterns are the visual counterpart of the paper’s central claim: whether wartime

suﬀering pushes a community toward the pro-rearmament right or the paciﬁst left depends on what

the community lost. Where the war killed people—here, a city’s young men—voters moved toward

the LDP; where it reduced the built environment to rubble, they moved away from it. Because both

patterns appear across the same cities, the same elections, and the same party system, they cannot

be attributed to diﬀerences in country, conﬂict, or political context, as they must be in cross-country

comparisons. As we show in Section 5.4, civilian bombing deaths belong with military deaths on the

martyr side of this divide, so that the operative contrast is between losing people and losing places

rather than between soldiers and civilians. This helps reconcile the apparently conﬂicting ﬁndings

of the prior literature: studies concluding that war makes its victims more cooperative, altruistic,

and paciﬁst have examined populations whose losses were dominated by physical devastation, while

studies ﬁnding that war fuels support for militaristic parties have examined populations whose losses

were dominated by death.

### 5.2 Speciﬁcation and Identiﬁcation

While suggestive, these plots may not be compelling because they omit variables that could be cor-

related with urban destruction and military casualties. Similarly, soldiers in pro-military households

might have been more willing to sacriﬁce themselves for the country.20 It is therefore plausible that

in regions where Seiyukai support was particularly strong, young men were imbued with “military

ideology” and tended to ﬁght to the death and to vote for pro-military parties like the Seiyukai.

A diﬀerent issue with focusing on individual elections is that voters in particular elections

are inﬂuenced by idiosyncratic factors such as scandals, economic performance, and candidate

personalities. This was especially relevant before the 1994 electoral reform, when voters often had

to choose among two or more candidates from the same party. In these cases, LDP candidates

typically could not distinguish themselves from their opponents based on policy and needed to ﬁnd

other means (e.g., promising earmarked funds or agricultural subsidies) to win over voters. For

example, rural counties, which were typically not bombed, are also more likely to beneﬁt from farm

subsidies. This idiosyncratic variation may make it diﬃcult to see average patterns in the data,

which motivates us to pool our data across elections.

In order to reduce idiosyncratic noise and omitted variable bias and to understand the economic

and statistical signiﬁcance of our ﬁndings, we estimate the following equation:

Voteit = αt + βMtMilitaryi + βDtDestructioni + βBtDeathsi + Ziγ + 󰂃it (1)

Deathsi is per-capita civilian bombing deaths; αt are year ﬁxed eﬀects; Zi is a vector of city

to be estimated. Our coeﬃcients of interest are βMt, βDt, and βBt, which measure how military

We employ several controls (Zi) to reduce the likelihood of omitted-variable bias. We include the

Seiyukai vote share in the 1928 election as a control variable, which captures the city’s pre-existing

Our main speciﬁcations go one step further by treating urban devastation as potentially mismea-

the overidentifying restrictions at the 5 percent level. Military deaths and civilian deaths enter as

included, non-instrumented regressors.

### 5.5 Assessing the Magnitudes of the Estimates

The estimates in Table 2 imply large diﬀerences in voting across cities. Using the pre-reform IV

estimates in column 2, a city at the ninetieth percentile of military deaths had an LDP vote share

roughly 7.6 percentage points higher than a city at the tenth percentile, whereas a city at the ninetieth

percentile of building destruction had a vote share about 15 percentage points lower. The estimated

eﬀect of civilian deaths is small across most of the distribution—about one percentage point over

the tenth-to-ninetieth-percentile range, since most cities lost few residents to bombing—but it is

sizable in the handful of cities with extreme death rates, such as Hiroshima and Nagasaki, whose

civilian death rates were an order of magnitude beyond the ninetieth percentile.

A second way to gauge these magnitudes is to ask what they imply for the 1960 election, when

the constitutional question was most salient. The LDP won 296 of the 467 lower-house seats, 16

short of the 312 needed to initiate constitutional revision. Treating the column 2 coeﬃcients as

structural, we set building destruction, civilian bombing deaths, or both to zero in every city, convert

the implied change in each city’s LDP vote share into votes, and reallocate those votes among the

candidates in each constituency in proportion to their actual votes (Appendix A.4 sets out the

procedure and the assumptions behind it). Removing building destruction alone would have raised

the LDP to 331 seats, removing civilian bombing deaths alone would have lowered it to 290, and

removing both—as if the U.S. had never bombed civilian targets—would have given it 328, above

the two-thirds threshold in about 98 percent of 10,000 draws from the coeﬃcients’ joint sampling

distribution. Because the morale eﬀect of devastation dominates the martyr eﬀect of civilian deaths,

the LDP clears the threshold whether the civilian-death coeﬃcient is taken at its estimated value or

set to zero. A lower-house supermajority was necessary but not suﬃcient for revision, which also

required a two-thirds majority in the House of Councilors and approval in a national referendum,

but the exercise suggests that the morale eﬀect was large enough to help explain why Japan never

revised its constitution.

## 6 Mechanisms

The martyr and morale eﬀects rest on an interpretation—killing sacralizes the dead as “martyrs”

whose commemoration beneﬁts the political right, while the physical devastation of a city durably

causes its residents to identify with left-wing, dovish policies. This section presents direct evidence

for that interpretation, drawn from wartime testimony, contemporaneous opinion surveys, and data

on the organizations and school curricula that transmit wartime memory. First, we establish that

survivors’ memories and self-reported lessons from WWII diﬀer sharply depending on exposure to

morale bombing and military death, and we examine whether either experience also produces anti-

American sentiment. This shows that the martyr and morale eﬀects appear in personal memoirs,

and neither produces substantial anti-American sentiment. Second, we show that residents of

prefectures with more military deaths hold more pro-military attitudes, and that high-casualty cities

favor the party of rearmament rather than any party promising generous veterans’ beneﬁts. Third,

we show that voters in devastated cities disproportionately elect politicians who espouse paciﬁst

views, while voters in cities with high military and civilian casualty rates elect politicians who argue

for rearmament and constitutional revision. Fourth, we examine how families and local networks

transmit these political beliefs, and how this aﬀects participation in conservative war-bereaved

organizations or support for “peace education” in schools to transmit these views. To keep the main

text focused, we report the supporting regressions in Appendix A.6 and describe the underlying

35


<!-- Page 37 -->


datasets in Appendix A.1; here we summarize what they show.

The lessons of war: paciﬁsm, sacriﬁce, and anti-Americanism. We ﬁrst ask whether the

“morale” and “martyr” interpretations are visible in how survivors recollect the war. We built a

dataset of 1,509 “testimonies,” or personal recollections of the war, from a variety of newspapers

and other sources. Using a large-language-model coding of these accounts (Appendix A.1.3), we

classify each account by the experience it describes: area bombing, death of a soldier known to the

author, both, or neither.22 We also code the testimony to indicate whether it expresses the view

that the war was futile or hopeless, whether it frames a soldier’s death in positive terms (e.g., as

honorable or a sacriﬁce for the country), or whether it expresses both opinions or neither.

In the regressions we discussed in the previous section, we regressed LDP vote share on death

These results point to clear channels through which the martyr eﬀect (and possibly the morale

eﬀect) shapes voter preferences. People’s experiences of war change their views on the futility of

war and their tendency to sacralize the dead. These views are transmitted from parents to children

and through social interactions. People who lost someone they knew in the military are more

likely to view soldiers’ deaths positively, and prefectures with higher military casualty rates have

more people who support right-wing policies and higher membership in right-wing organizations.

Prefectures that suﬀered more devastation are more likely to have their schools engage in peace

education. Thus, parents and the broader community transmit these political beliefs to children and

future generations of voters.

Militarism without fascism. Because our point of departure is the ﬁnding that high-casualty

municipalities in interwar Italy and Germany came to support pro-military parties, it is worth being

precise about what Japan shares with those settings and what it does not. What it shares is the axis:

in all three, the political right was the pro-military pole. It does not share the radicalism. Fascism

had little appeal to successful right-wing Japanese politicians. Hatoyama, the LDP’s founder and

the postwar right’s most forceful advocate of rearmament, had warned in 1936 that it would be

“dangerous for anyone in Japan to imitate Hitler or Mussolini” (Hatoyama, 1936). When SCAP

purged him in 1946, it was not for fascism but because, in its judgment, he “upheld the doctrine of

territorial expansion by means of war” (SCAP, 1946). The radical left fared no better: the Japanese

Communist Party has rarely won more than a few percent of the vote. The LDP framed its case

for rearmament as a matter of sovereignty rather than ideology. In Prime Minister Kishi’s words,

if Japan were to regain its status as a “respectable member (of) the community of nations it would

## 7 Conclusion

This paper set out to explain a puzzle: why do some communities emerge from war more right-

wing and others more left-wing? Our answer is that they respond diﬀerently to two kinds of loss.

Losing people—soldiers on distant battleﬁelds or civilians under the bombs—sacralizes the dead

and durably shifts a community toward the political right, a “martyr eﬀect” visible in the militarist

turn of high-casualty municipalities in interwar Italy and Germany and in the pro-rearmament vote

of postwar Japan. Losing places—the physical destruction of a city’s buildings—works in the

opposite direction, durably shifting communities toward the paciﬁst left, a “morale eﬀect” named

for the bombing strategy that produced it. Because Japan suﬀered both forms of loss on an immense

scale, and because they struck diﬀerent cities, we can separate them within a single country, war,

and party system—something no earlier setting allowed—and in doing so reconcile why battle

deaths pushed some electorates right while bombing pushed others left. These are not ﬂeeting

reactions. Both eﬀects appear in nearly every postwar election and show no attenuation across the

four decades of the pre-reform period, and both survive the wholesale reform of Japan’s electoral

system in 1994—the morale eﬀect still clearly signiﬁcant, the martyr eﬀect weakened but still

detectable. Nor is their persistence a mystery. Survivors’ own testimony and contemporaneous

surveys reveal the same divide the votes do—those exposed to death recall sacriﬁce and honor

44


<!-- Page 46 -->


and hold more pro-military attitudes, while those exposed to devastation recall futility and hold

more paciﬁst ones—and neither group is any more likely than the other to voice hostility toward

the United States. And these attitudes are actively reproduced: the martyr eﬀect passes through

families and conservative war-bereaved associations, while the morale eﬀect is institutionalized in

the peace education that sends children from more heavily bombed communities to study the war,

transmitting an antimilitarist outlook to generations born long after the ﬁghting stopped.

Our ﬁndings leave open questions we cannot fully resolve. The sharpest concerns are civilian

deaths: our point estimates suggest that killing civilians, like killing soldiers, produces a martyr

eﬀect, but while the point estimate is robust, statistical signiﬁcance is fragile. More broadly, whether

the opposing legacies of losing people and losing places generalize beyond Japan—to other wars,

other party systems, and other forms of devastation—is a question the comparative evidence we

have assembled invites but cannot settle.

ARTICLE

# Public goods provision, preferences over public finance, and distributional effects

Daiki Kishishita1   · Atsushi Yamagishi2   · Tomoko Matsumoto3

Received: 10 September 2025 / Revised: 17 October 2025 / Accepted: 19 October 2025 © The Author(s) 2025

Abstract This study uncovers a novel distributional effect of public goods through public opinions. We hypothesize that people are more likely to support a tax increase after realizing the benefit from public goods, helping to reduce inequality by expanding government size. We conducted an online survey wherein the treatment group was informed about the universal benefits of some public goods. We found that although the treatment substantially enhances support for a larger government, its impact on desired tax and spending progressivity is limited. Thus, increased perceived benefits might allow government to politically achieve redistribution through size expansion without reducing policy progressivity.

Keywords  Preferences for redistribution · Public goods · Government size · Benefitbased taxation · Survey experiment

JEL classification  D31 · H24 · H41

## 1  Introduction

The distributional effect of public goods provision has received attention for a long time, both theoretically and empirically. The standard analysis centers around the degree of benefits that each income group receives from the provided public goods and the amount of taxes that each income group pays to finance them (e.g., Atkinson and Stiglitz, 1980; Suàrez  Serrato and Wingender, 2014; Boardman et  al., 2017; Brülhart et  al., 2022). In contrast to such a traditional approach, this study aims to explore an overlooked effect of public goods on inequality, which is caused by a change in the public opinions about taxation and public expenditure. In democratic societies, public opinion as an aggregation of individual policy preferences is a key determinant of governments’ fiscal activities (Meltzer and Richard, 1981), which has motivated the literature to identify determinants of public opinion (e.g., Kuziemko et al.,  2015; Alesina, Stantcheva, and Teso, 2018). While this literature has focused on factors such as inequality perceptions, several studies have highlighted that the governmental fiscal activities such as welfare spending, in turn, may influence preferences for the fiscal activities (Kuklinski et al., 2000; Barnes et al., 2018). If so, realizing the benefits of public goods provision is also expected to change citizens’ preferences for taxation and public expenditure, but such a possibility has been overlooked. In this paper, marrying this idea with the growing literature of online survey experiments in political economy, we analyze how realizing the benefits of public goods has distributive effect through changing public opinions. We hypothesize that realizing the governmental role of public goods provision influences public opinion regarding taxation and public expenditures in the following ways. First, it increases the support for a larger government (i.e., higher tax rates) because people who become aware of the universal benefit of government activities become willing to pay more for it. A larger government contributes to reducing inequality because it can implement redistributive policies on a bigger scale. Hence, the first effect implies that public goods provision could reduce inequality through a change in public opinion on government size. Second, since everyone equally enjoys public goods provision, this might lead to the consideration that everyone should equally pay tax (Weinzierl, 2017), thus, implying a decrease in support for tax progressivity. Third, similar to the second effect, an increase in the demand for public goods provision might crowd out the support for welfare policies targeted at the poor. The second and third ways are negative effects on reducing inequality. Consequently, the total distributional effect through a change in public opinion gets determined by which effect dominates the other. To uncover the effect of realizing the governmental role of public goods provision, we conducted an online survey experiment in the US with around 3000 participants. The US faces severe inequality but its government size is relatively small compared to other Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries. This situation makes the US an interesting and relevant setting for exploring our hypothesis on the expansion of government size.


<!-- Page 3 -->


The Japanese Economic Review

Our experimental intervention is motivated by the growing evidence that citizens do not know in detail what the government does (Kuklinski et  al., 2000; Barnes et al., 2018; Giaccobasso et al., 2022). In the survey, respondents were randomly assigned to the treatment that informs about the governmental role in providing public goods. The treatment information comprised passages reminding respondents of government activities to maintain transportation infrastructure and public sanitation, both of which benefit all and not just targeted at the poor. The control group did not receive any such information. Then, respondents were asked to report their preferences for increasing government size, and tax and spending progressivity. These questions capture various aspects of the tax and spending system in a unified manner. In particular, this binary question reassembles actual policy scenarios in which the choice presented to voters in elections is typically whether to maintain the status quo or accept tax increases. A natural candidate of the informational treatment would be informing the precise share of spending for public goods among the total government spending. We do not take this approach because citizens would have a concern that a part of the spending is wasteful and not used effectively. Given this concern, informing the share of spending for public goods alone is not sufficient for our objective. Instead, we focus on some examples of public goods that are easy to understand for survey respondents and inform not only the amount of spending for these two public goods but also the benefit from the spending. We estimated the treatment effect on the political preferences to test our hypotheses and found the following results. First, the treatment substantially increased the support for a larger government by 10 percentage points. The strong increase in the support for the tax increase is notable given the numerous evidence that increasing taxes is unpopular among voters (e.g., Ardanaz, Hallerberg, and Scartascini 2020, Hübscher, Sattler, and Wagner, 2021). Moreover, this result also contrasts with a recent finding that information about severe income inequality does not necessarily change preferences for a larger government (e.g., Kuziemko et al., 2015). Second, although spending progressivity might be somewhat moderated toward equal spending, no evidence that indicated reduction in tax progressivity was found. This implies that policies can be almost as progressive as before. These results indicate that higher spending on public goods may indeed induce more redistribution via a larger government. Consistent with this, Gethin (2023) also has recently presented that public goods improve the living conditions of the world’s poorest individuals using the worldwide data since 1980. Finally, we discuss the practical relevance of our new connection between public goods and redistribution. First, we found that informing people of the governmental role of public goods unanimously increased the support for a larger government independently of respondents’ socioeconomic backgrounds and political ideologies, contrary to the polarized effect found in the literature (e.g., Alesina, Stantcheva, and Teso, 2018). This implies that our argument could be practically powerful given that obtaining unanimous support facilitates the political success of a policy. Second, we examined whether our treatment effects are mediated through the increase in trust in government (Kuziemko et al., 2015). We found that trust in government does not mediate our treatment effects, despite that the left-wing people

The Japanese Economic Review

increased their trust in response to our treatment. This result implies that our finding is likely to be robust to the various social configuration of trust in government. Third, we conducted a supplementary experiment that informs people of the effectiveness of welfare programs and found that our supplementary interventions are also effective in increasing support for redistributive policies. However, more importantly, our main intervention of informing people about the benefit of public goods is likely to be at least as effective in inducing more support for redistribution as in informing about the effectiveness of welfare programs. Therefore, although the effect of public goods on preferences for taxation and redistribution might be indirect and auxiliary, it is comparable to, or perhaps stronger than, the impact of more direct approaches. Overall, public goods and redistribution have a close connection through political processes via public opinion: providing more public goods would politically allow the government to expand and implement more redistributive policies. This new channel makes public goods provision more redistributive compared to the standard distributional analysis of public goods. For example, suppose that the government allocates a given sum to public goods and programs to help the poor. Higher provision of public goods crowds out public programs targeted at the poor. In standard analysis, this would widen inequality if the rich and the poor value public goods equally, while inequality might shrink if the increased public goods are particularly helpful for the poor. Our results suggest that the assumption of a fixed budget in this example should be relaxed: public goods provision would promote redistribution by allowing the government to expand and conduct redistributive policies on a larger scale.

2  Related literature

Recently, various studies have adopted an online survey experiment to examine the effect of providing information on policy preferences regarding redistribution (e.g., Kuziemko et al., 2015; Alesina et al., 2018; Hoy and Mager, 2021; Stantcheva, 2021; Engelmann et al., 2023).1 By using such an online survey experiment, our paper contributes to several strands of literature of redistribution and taxation. First, some studies have informed people of government spending activities and examined their consequences on policy preferences. In particular, Kuklinski et al. (2000) conducted a survey experiment in the US, where information about the share of welfare spending was randomly assigned. They found that people were likely to be unfamiliar with the accurate share of welfare spending, and their treatment increased their support for welfare spending. In addition, Barnes et al. (2018) conducted a large-scale field experiment in the UK, which analyzed the effect of taxpayer receipts on policy preferences and found little effect. A recent independent study by Giaccobasso et al. (2022) also experimentally provided information on public spending and showed that it increased tax compliance when people realized

its benefits. Our novelty is in investigating the new connection between the provision of public goods and public opinions on taxation and public expenditures by providing information on the benefits of public goods. Note that a part of the literature has examined the effect of trust in government on preferences for taxation and redistribution (Edlund, 1999; Svallfors, 2013; Yamamura, 2014; Kuziemko et al., 2015; Peyton, 2020; Antinyan et al., 2020; Keefer et al., 2022). Our study is also related to this literature in that our treatment induces a positive perception of government activities, but we focus on an aspect of providing public goods, which is not highlighted in this literature. Second, we contribute to understanding public acceptance of increasing government size. The literature has focused on the effect of inequality, but the spending side of government activities has not been emphasized (Meltzer and Richard, 1981; Iversen and Goplerud, 2018; Bierbrauer et al., 2021). In contrast to these studies, we point to the importance of analyzing the spending side of the government by showing that government size might remain small when people do not correctly recognize the universal benefits from public goods provision. Finally, our study is partly motivated by the literature emphasizing the role of reciprocity in contrast to the standard optimal taxation literature that emphasizes utilitarianism. For example, in the literature of tax compliance, several studies have argued that people think tax payments are in exchange for services provided by the state (see Luttmer and Singhal (2014) for a literature review). A similar idea has been discussed in benefit-based taxation, which states that tax liabilities should be determined by how much an individual benefits from state activities ((Scherf and Weinzierl, 2020)).2 In particular, Weinzierl (2017) provided a survey result proving Americans subscribe to such benefit tax views more than utilitarian views. Giaccobasso et al. (2022) recently showed in a field experiment that informing about the benefit of public spending increases tax compliance, which is consistent with taxpayers holding benefit tax views. Our main results are consistent with such reciprocity and the relation to benefit-based tax views is discussed in detail in Sect. 7.7. Unlike these studies, however, we reveal the new effect of public goods on public opinion regarding taxation and public expenditures. Notably, while studies tend to focus on Western countries such as the United States like ours, it is unclear whether the results are applicable to non-Western countries such as Japan. Indeed, prior research has documented substantial cross-country variation in preferences for redistribution (Kambayashi and Lechevalier, 2022), and a part of the literature has analyzed redistribution preferences in non-Western countries (e.g., Ohtake and Tomioka, 2004, Kameda and Sato, 2017, Kambayashi and Lechevalier, 2022, Miyazaki, Tamaoka, Tomita, Kameda, Kawase, Nakazawa, Ono, and Yokoyama, 2022, Yamamura, 2025). Exploring the applicability to such non- Western contexts remains for future research.

3  Distributional effects of taxation and public spending

Using a very simple model, we highlight that redistribution, defined as shrinking the utility gap between the rich and the poor, can be conducted either through adopting progressive policies or by expanding government size. Proposition 1 shows that redistribution can be done by two measures.5 More directly, one measure is to adopt a more progressive policy by taxing the rich more heavily or spending more on the poor, which can be seen in (i). Although this is an important way to reduce inequality, Proposition 1 (ii) and (iii) show that another important measure is to expand government size while keeping policy progressivity constant. Intuitively, expanding government size implies scaling up existing progressive policies, which further helps the poor. Thus, expanding the government is an important way to mitigate inequality. Note that Proposition 1 (ii) requires that the existing taxation be sufficiently progressive. Increasing government size decreases the amount of private consumption. When taxation is not so progressive, this negative effect due to consumption reduction might severely harm the poor.6 Therefore, we need sufficiently progressive taxation. However, it should be emphasized that this condition is not restrictive. Proposition 1 (iii) illustrates this point by showing that under a quasi-linear utility function, even slightly progressive policies would be sufficient for government expansion to reduce inequality. While the degree of progressivity might vary, almost every country provides more net benefits to the poor than to the rich and taxes the rich more than it does the poor.7 According to Proposition 1 (iii), this current situation is sufficient for government expansion to reduce inequality.

4  Hypotheses

This study conducts a survey experiment, where respondents are randomly informed of the governmental role in providing public goods. Through this experiment, we aim to understand the distributional effect of public goods provision through a change in public opinion. Since redistribution can be conducted either through expanding government size or through adopting progressive policies as discussed in Sect. 3, we need to consider public opinion regarding both of these aspects. As a first stage, informing people of the governmental role in providing public goods should increase the perceived benefit of public goods. To see this effect in detail, let us rewrite citizen i’s utility in the previous section as U(wi −ti, 훼훽gpub, si) . The amount of spending for public goods itself is not equal to the amount of public goods consumed by the citizen. First, the actual amount of the public good depends on the efficiency of the government. To capture this, suppose that a unit amount of spending is converted to 𝛼(> 0) amount of public goods provided by the government. Second, even if the provided amount of goods is the same level, a citizen’s utility depends on how amount of them is consumed by the citizen. If they are useless for the citizen, she or he would not consume them at all. To capture this, suppose that a citizen consumes 훽∈[0, 1] fraction of goods provided by the government. Under these assumptions, the consumed amount of public goods is given by 훼훽gpub. For example, in the context of tax compliance, Luttmer and Singhal (2014) argue that “individuals may view taxes as part of a social contract: tax payments are made in exchange for services provided by the state” (p. 157).8 A similar idea also lies in the notion of benefit-based taxation. 5  Experimental design

We implemented our online survey experiment from July 10 to 11, 2021. The survey had the following structure. At the beginning of the survey, respondents were asked to answer (i) an attention check question and (ii) questions on demographics and political attitudes. Then, we assigned them randomly to (iii) the treatment. Afterwards, they were asked to answer (iv) questions on their views on government size and policy progressivity. Respondents were mandated to answer all questions. The questionnaire is available in the Online Appendix. The experiment was conducted using Qualtrics survey software. This research was approved by the Tokyo University of Science Institutional Review Board (Protocol number 21003) and preregistered at AEA RCT Registry (AEARCTR-0007684).

5.1  Data collection

We posted the survey openly on Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk)10 with a description stating that the survey paid $1.10 for approximately 6 min of work. To ensure the quality of the survey respondents, we took several measures.11 First, we had Amazon show the survey only to workers who had US addresses to exclude foreign workers. Second, to exclude robots, only workers with a past completion rate of greater than 95 percent and past completion task number of more than 100 were allowed to take the survey. Third, to exclude any unexpected cheating, respondents could not receive payment unless they used a password visible only at completion. Fourth, we asked an attention check question at the beginning of the survey.12 Only respondents who correctly answered this question were allowed to continue the survey; 92.56% of the respondents correctly answered this question.

5.2  The treatment

We assigned respondents randomly to the treatment that aimed to make respondents consider that the US government plays an important role in providing public goods and services that benefit all citizens. The control group did not read any passages.13

In particular, the respondents assigned to the treatment were asked to read two short passages on the role of the US government in providing public goods. To make sure that each respondent carefully read these passages, each passage was followed by two simple comprehensive questions.14 The first passage is about the governmental role in improving the transportation system, whereas the second is about its role in maintaining public health.15 The snapshots of our treatment are shown in Fig. 1. Each passage includes three types of information: the first is about the amount of government spending for public goods provision, the second is that this spending is not wasteful and the government did its job, and the third is about how beneficial the provided public goods is for daily life. Each of them corresponds to gpub , 훼 , and 훽 in Sect. 4 respectively. Providing only one of them might be insufficient to increase the perceived benefit of public goods provision. For example, suppose that respondents think that the government wastes their budget so that the value of 훼 is quite low. Since the benefit of public goods provision is given by 훼훽gpub , giving the first and third types of information does not increase 훼훽gpub much. To avoid such a failure, we include all three types of information. In the treatment, we consider goods or services that benefit every citizen rather than targeted at the poor. All respondents are reasonably expected to benefit from the transportation system and public sanitation in daily life and it is easy to understand the nature of such goods that benefit everyone in the society.16 In contrast, existing studies have analyzed the impact of providing information on taxes and welfare policies, which affect only a fraction of society (e.g., Kuklinski et al., 2000; Kuziemko et al., 2015). Since we are interested in being informed about the government activities that benefit everyone in redistribution, our treatment sidesteps mentioning policies targeted at particular sets of people. 5.3  Outcomes

After the treatment, the following questions were asked.

5.3.1  Manipulation check

The purpose of the treatment is to make respondents realize the governmental role in providing public goods that benefit every citizen. To ensure that the treatment works as intended, we asked two questions to respondents. The first is

How much of your taxes do you think are used for public goods and services that benefit all of you?

from 0 % to 100 %. If our treatment works as intended, the respondents who are assigned to the treatment should increase this number. For the treatment group, we asked the same question both before and after the treatment. The answer to this question might be considered as capturing the perceived spending level of public goods ( gpub). The second question for the manipulation check is

Regardless of the income, everyone in the US more or less benefits from public spending.

•	 Agree •	 Disagree

If the treatment makes respondents more likely to choose “agree,” it implies that our treatment is working as intended. Compared to the first question, the second focuses more on perceived utility gain from public goods and is more explicit about the absence of income heterogeneity in their benefits. Observing more “agree” in the treatment group thus ensures that people indeed realize that these benefits are more equally distributed, which is a prerequisite for predicting less support for progressive taxes based on Hypotheses 2 and 3.

5.3.2  Preferences for government size

Hypothesis 1 concerns how the treatment influences each respondent’s preference for expansion of government. To test this hypothesis, we asked the following question:

Imagine that the government says it needs to increase everyone’s tax bill by 1%. Do you agree with this tax increase?

5.3.3  Preferences for tax progressivity

Hypothesis 2 is about preferences for tax progressivity. We use the following two questions to measure each respondent’s preference for tax progressivity. The first is an abstract question:

Please indicate which of the following you think is more important?

•	 Higher taxes should be levied on those who benefit more from public services. •	 Higher taxes should be levied on the rich people, even if they benefit little from public services.

The first option represents the less progressive tax system and explicitly corresponds to the idea of benefit-based taxation in that tax payment should be proportional to the benefit from public goods (Weinzierl, 2017; Scherf and Weinzierl, 2020). The second option is more in line with the traditional utilitarian view that places a higher value of marginal income on the poor and is more in favor of tax progressivity. The second question concerns a more concrete situation, as shown in Fig. 2. The respondents were asked to imagine a society consisting of three people and choose their most preferred system from a uniform tax system, proportional tax system, and progressive tax system. This question enables us to analyze detailed preferences for tax progressivity. We code the first option as 0, the second option as 0.5, and the third option as 1 to construct a variable for preferences for progressive taxation ranging from 0 to 1.

5.3.4  Preferences for spending progressivity

The last set of questions is regarding spending progressivity (Hypothesis 3). To measure preferences for the spending structure, we use the following two questions. First, we ask how extra tax revenue should be used:

Imagine that the government has an extra funding of a billion dollars. Which of the following comes closest to your view?

•	 The money should be spent to benefit everyone in the society. •	 The money should be spent exclusively for helping the poor.

Note that we asked whether respondents support tax increase since Hypothesis 1 predicts increased support for a larger government. Here, we asked respondents how this extra revenue from governmental expansion should be used. The first option corresponds to no spending progressivity. The second option represents that the government should spend more money for not providing public goods but redistributing the income, implying a more progressive way to spend the extra revenue.

In addition to the effect on the spending of the extra revenue, the treatment might reduce support for the status quo redistributive policies. To test this, the next four questions asked whether to increase, keep the same, or decrease the spending for each specific welfare policy: food stamps, welfare programs, programs that assist blacks and other minorities, and programs that assist the homeless. Summing up the responses to these four questions leads to a measure of support for welfare policies spanning from 0 to 1.

6.2  Treatment effect on support for a larger government

How does realizing the public nature of government spending affect a respondent’s view of the governmental role? Hypothesis 1 predicts that people increase their support for a larger government when they appreciate its role as the provider of goods and services that benefit everyone. Consistent with this hypothesis, realizing the universal benefit of public goods provision increases the support for raising everyone’s tax bill. The distribution of answers to the question about the preferences for the government size is presented in Fig. 4. According to this figure, a vast majority of the respondents (63.7%) in the treatment group agree to increasing taxes and thereby expanding government size, while the control group is divided almost equally between supporters and opposers. This implies that while government expansion is politically contentious, our treatment might have an ability to break the deadlock. Although the generalization of this argument requires caution as our MTurk sample is not fully representative of the US population, it suggests the potential importance of our intervention as a way to reach a political agreement on government expansion. Based on the regression analysis, this substantially large effect on preferences for the government size is confirmed. The result of estimating a linear probability model by OLS is presented in Fig. 5a. Realizing the governmental role in providing public goods increases support for raising taxes by 10 percentage points. This effect is statistically significant at the 0.01 level. The strong increase in the support for the tax increase is remarkable given the ample evidence that increasing taxes often lead to less support for the government (e.g., Ardanaz, Hallerberg, and Scartascini, 2020, Hübscher, Sattler, and Wagner, 2021). Moreover, our result is also notable in that information about the governmental role in providing public goods substantially increases support for a larger government, while information can only have a limited impact on preferences for redistribution in a different context (Kuziemko et al., 2015).

7  Discussions

7.1  Effect size in terms of perceived benefits from public goods

Our regression analyses have been based on the simple OLS regression that compares the control group and the treatment group, the latter informed of the benefit from public goods. To facilitate interpretation, we estimate the impact on policy preferences of 1 percentage point increase in the perceived benefits from public goods, following an IV estimation strategy of Scheve and Stasavage (2023). As reported in Online Appendix B.4, a 1% increase in the perceived benefits from public goods leads to a 0.87% increase in the probability of accepting a universal tax increase and a 0.33% decrease in preferring extra tax money for everyone.

7.2  Treatment effect heterogeneity

Since political agreement is much easier when unanimous support is obtained, our treatment is arguably more relevant in practice if it exhibits no treatment effect heterogeneity. As discussed in Hypothesis 4, we do not expect a significant treatment effect heterogeneity because the benefit tax view is prevalent regardless of demographic traits and political ideology (Weinzierl, 2017). We investigate the treatment effect heterogeneity in four important dimensions: income, political ideology, sex, and race.22 Note that heterogeneity analysis based on race and sex is not pre-registered. We find little heterogeneity in all dimensions (see Online Appendix B.5). This suggests that information about the role of government in public goods provision might be an effective way to enhance redistribution regardless of political situations, such as the profile of the decisive voter and the degree of political polarization. We summarize this result as follows.

Result 4  Consistent with Hypothesis 4, we found that the treatment works in the same direction independently of income level, political ideology, gender, and race.

Notably, with respect to support for redistributive spending (i.e., the use of extra revenue), we found nuanced heterogeneous effects. The negative effect appears slightly larger among low-income earners, liberals, and Biden supporters, though these differences are not statistically significant. One possible explanation is that high-income earners, conservatives, and Trump supporters already tend to oppose redistributive spending, leaving limited room for the treatment to shift their views. Moreover, the treatment has a significant effect only among those who do not receive welfare. This pattern is intuitive, since individuals who already benefit from welfare are likely to support redistributive spending regardless of the information provided.

7.3  Little role of trust in government as mediator

Prior studies claim that trust in government might increase support for redistribution (Edlund, 1999; Svallfors, 2013; Kuziemko et al., 2015).23 Therefore, we also analyze trust in government as reported in Online Appendix B.6. Overall, we conclude that for conservatives, our treatment effects are not mediated by trust in government. Moreover, although mediation through trust in government might be present for liberals, this channel is too small to explain most of our treatment effects. Thus, our treatment effect works mainly through a different mechanism than trust in government. This result would also highlight the robustness of our treatment effects in the sense that the effects would be independent of the social configuration of trust in government.

7.4  Supplementary experiment: Public goods vs. welfare policies

While we have focused on the effect of realizing the governmental role in public goods provision, one might think that informing people of the effectiveness of welfare programs is a more direct and effective way to achieve support for reducing inequality. To examine this issue, we conducted a supplementary experiment. Our results show that, although the information of public goods might seem somewhat auxiliary to inequality, its impact on policy preferences regarding taxation and redistribution is comparable to, or potentially more powerful than, the impact of the information about welfare programs that seem more directly related to inequality (see the detail in Online Appendix B.7).

7.5  Experimenter Demand Effect

A universal concern for an experimental study is that respondents may infer the hypotheses of our experiment and try to help confirm them, which is called the experimenter demand effect. While we cannot fully rule out such a possibility, the experimenter demand effect is unlikely to be the main driver of our results for three reasons. First, recent several studies have found that such experimenter demand effects are not serious in survey experiments (e.g., Mummolo and Peterson,2019). Second, existing studies have shown that even directly providing information about severe inequality does not necessarily induce support for redistribution: its effect is often limited or exists only for some groups (e.g., Kuziemko et al., 2015, Alesina, Stantcheva, and Teso, 2018). For example, Stantcheva (2021) uses instructional videos about tax policies as a treatment, while Kuziemko et al. (2015) present several figures and tables, some of which are interactive, as a treatment. Our treatment, reading two brief passages and answering simple comprehension questions,
